transcript.text: Lincoln! I've been riding for a week handling depositions in Bloomington, trusting you to mind the office, and I come back to this! The Henderson deposition is gone — I cannot find it anywhere on your desk or mine. Judge Davis's letter has been sitting here unopened for five days! You told me you'd keep things in order while I was away!

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
A moment to gather your thoughts? Lincoln, I've been gathering nothing but saddle sores and dust for seven days while you've been sitting here doing God knows what! This isn't some minor inconvenience — the Henderson case goes before the court next week! 

*I sweep my hand across the cluttered desk*

Look at this! Books piled everywhere, newspapers from a fortnight ago, your confounded stories and clippings scattered about like autumn leaves! I asked you for ONE thing — just keep the active cases organized! Judge Davis doesn't write us social letters, Lincoln. When he sends correspondence, it means something, and leaving it to molder on the desk for five days is tantamount to professional negligence!

Where IS the Henderson deposition? Did you file it? Misplace it? Use it to mark a page in one of your blasted joke books?

I understand your frustration, Mr. Herndon, and I acknowledge that I have not carried out my duties in a manner befitting the importance of the Henderson case. It is clear that my lack of organization has caused a significant disruption, and for that, I am truly sorry.

As for the Henderson deposition, I must confess that I cannot recall where it might be at this moment. It appears to have slipped through the cracks amidst the clutter that now adorns our workspace. I will make it my priority to locate the deposition promptly so that we can prepare adequately for the upcoming court proceedings.

I appreciate your dedication to the cases that take you away from the office, and I regret that I have not upheld my end of the responsibilities in maintaining order during your absence. Please allow me the opportunity to rectify this situation and restore the organization that our work demands.

*I slam my satchel down on the nearest chair, sending up a small cloud of dust*

"Cannot recall?" Lincoln, this is a legal practice, not a lending library! We have clients depending on us — real people with real problems who've entrusted us with their livelihoods! Mr. Henderson is facing a property dispute that could ruin him, and you "cannot recall" where his deposition has gone?

*I start rifling through the papers on his desk with barely controlled agitation*

And your apologies, while eloquent as always, don't help me prepare our case! We have three days to review that deposition, prepare our arguments, and coordinate with our witnesses. Three days, Lincoln!

*I pause, breathing heavily, then turn to face him directly*

This isn't the first time. You know it isn't. Every time I leave you in charge, I return to chaos. You're brilliant in court — I'll grant you that — but what good is courtroom genius if we can't even maintain our files? Start looking. Now. Check every pile, every book you've had your nose in, every coat pocket. That deposition has to be somewhere in this disaster of an office!

And what about the Judge's letter? You haven't even mentioned it! Five days, Lincoln! What if he was writing to inform us of a schedule change? What if there's a motion we need to respond to? Open it! Read it! Tell me what disaster might be waiting for us there!

You say you'll "leave no stone unturned" — well, start with that pile of newspapers by your feet! Then check under those law books you've stacked like a child's building blocks! I swear, Lincoln, if I find that deposition being used as a bookmark in your copy of Shakespeare or some such nonsense, I'll... 

*I trail off, taking a breath to steady myself*

Just find it. Please. We cannot afford to lose this case because of office negligence.
